lesson.title: Je n'ai pas mangé
lesson.subtitle: The sandwich wraps the auxiliary (je n'ai pas compris, tu n'as pas vu) and déjà slots inside.

hook.title: Where the Negation Sandwich Sits in the Passé Composé
hook.content: When a verb has two parts — the auxiliary (j'ai, tu as, je suis) and the past participle (mangé, compris, vu, allé) — the sandwich ALWAYS hugs the conjugated auxiliary, leaving the participle outside at the end: Je n'ai pas mangé, Je n'ai pas compris, Je n'ai jamais vu ce film, Je n'ai rien fait!

footnotes.title: Notice how English 'I have never seen / I have already eaten' uses the EXACT same slot!
footnotes.content: French puts pas, jamais, rien, and déjà in the exact same middle slot where English puts 'not / never / already' between 'have' and 'seen'!

pattern.title: Subject + ne + Auxiliary + pas/jamais/rien/déjà + Participle
pattern.content: Wrap the auxiliary, never the participle!
pattern.linguist_note: French negative and aspectual adverbs occupy the post-auxiliary position above the past participle.
pattern.trap_note: Never put pas, jamais, rien, or déjà after the participle (*Je n'ai compris pas) — slot them between the auxiliary and the participle!

exercises.prompt: Match each past negative or adverbial sentence with its meaning:

matching_pairs.german: Haven't you eaten? / Didn't you eat?

matching_pairs.english: Il n'a rien dit / rien fait

exercises.target_answer: I didn't understand / haven't understood, Haven't you eaten? / Didn't you eat?, I have never seen that, He said nothing / did nothing, We have already reserved
exercises.meaning: Je n'ai pas compris, Tu n'as pas mangé ?, Je n'ai jamais vu ça, Il n'a rien dit / rien fait, Nous avons déjà réservé
exercises.explanation: pas, jamais, rien, and déjà all stand between the auxiliary and the participle!

exercises.prompt: What is the literal word-for-word order of 'Je n'ai rien fait'?
exercises.meaning: Literal structure: I not-have nothing done
exercises.explanation: rien ('nothing') stands right between n'ai and the participle fait!

exercises.prompt: How do you say 'I have never visited Lyon'?
exercises.explanation: ne...jamais wraps the auxiliary ai, right before visité.

exercises.idea: I did not understand the question
cues: I not-have step → Je n'ai pas
understood the question → compris la question
exercises.target_answer: Je n'ai pas compris la question
exercises.meaning: I did not understand the question
exercises.explanation: n'ai pas hugs the auxiliary ai; compris follows after pas.

diagnosis.cue: Put pas between n'ai and compris: Je n'ai pas compris.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.spoken: Elle n'est pas venue hier soir
exercises.target_answer: Elle n'est pas venue hier soir
exercises.explanation: In the être house too, n'...pas wraps the auxiliary est: Elle n'est pas venue.
exercises.affirmation: You wrapped n'est pas around the auxiliary before venue!

summary.outcome: Position ne…pas, ne…jamais, ne…rien, and déjà around the auxiliary in the passé composé.

use_example.german: Je n'ai jamais vu ce film, mais j'ai déjà lu le livre.
use_example.english: I've never seen this movie, but I've already read the book.

summary.takeaway: In the past tense, pas, jamais, rien, and déjà always sit between the auxiliary and the participle.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on Le Pont ([5081] De matin à soir): see how Je n'ai pas mangé leads directly into De matin à soir.

twist.prompt: Think it through again without looking back — express "I did not understand the question" in French:
twist.target_answer: Je n'ai pas compris la question
twist.explanation: Re-constructing "Je n'ai pas compris la question" from the underlying rule cements the pattern of Je n'ai pas mangé.

mangé.etymology_derivation: manger ← Latin manducāre 'to chew'. English 'mange' is the eating disease — the verb came with the Normans' dogs.

compris.etymology_derivation: prendre → pris, comprendre → compris, apprendre → appris.

vu.context_translation: I have already seen this film.
vu.etymology_derivation: English already owns this participle inside 'déjà vu'!

pris.etymology_derivation: French uses prendre ('to take') for ordering food and drink, just like English 'I'll take a coffee'.

déjà.etymology_derivation: You already know it from déjà vu ('already seen').

pas.etymology_derivation: negation grew from ne vais pas un pas — 'I don't go a step'. Pas is literally a footstep, the same word as pace.

ne.etymology_derivation: Latin nōn wore down to ne. The verb sits in a ne...pas sandwich; spoken French often drops the first slice.

rien.etymology_derivation: Latin rem 'a thing' (root of real, republic). Just like pas ('a step'), a positive noun turned negative by company with ne.

jamais.etymology_derivation: Latin iam magis 'ever more'. Paired with ne, it means 'never'.

avoir.etymology_derivation: Latin habēre = have. The H dropped and stayed dropped — French never pronounces its Latin H.

ion.name: The -ION Bridge
ion.phonetic_rule: Spelling converts 1:1; the final N is nasalised — thought, not said (collection /kɔlɛksjɔ̃/).
ion.historical_linguistics: English absorbed thousands of Latin-dress nouns through Norman French and later Renaissance borrowing. The -tion/-sion endings are the single largest cognate landing zone between the two languages.
ion.philological_note: Every -ION noun is feminine, so the article is la — elided to l' before a vowel. The ending is a gender decoder, not a memory item.
ion.literature_source: Walter, Le français dans tous les sens (1988); Pope, From Latin to Modern French (1952).

ation.name: The -ation Engine
ation.historical_linguistics: French -er verbs descend from Latin -āre; the English -ation nouns and French verbs are two leaves of the same Latin branch, so the noun unlocks the verb with almost no loss.
ation.philological_note: The whole -ation goes — célébration → célébrer, never *célébrater. Test for the -ation noun in English first; it is the proof the verb converts.
ation.literature_source: Guillaume, Temps et verbe (1929); standard French morphophonology.

ite.name: The -ité Bridge
ite.phonetic_rule: English final -ity becomes stressed final -ité /ite/ — the é marks the syllable English swallows.
ite.historical_linguistics: Latin -itās survives in English -ity and French -ité; both are bookish layers grafted onto the everyday vocabulary, which is why they convert with no sound loss.
ite.philological_note: All -ité nouns are feminine (la possibilité, la liberté).
ite.literature_source: Pope (1952); Brunot, Histoire de la langue française.

ance.name: The -ance/-ence Twins
ance.phonetic_rule: Same spelling family; the AN is nasal: différence /difeʁɑ̃s/.
ance.historical_linguistics: Latin -antia/-entia produced English -ance/-ence and French -ance/-ence directly; the pair is one of the highest-conversion zones in the vocabulary.

e.name: The é/ed Twins
e.phonetic_rule: The past participle in -é /e/ is the English -ed: mangé/manged, décidé/decided, marié/married.
e.historical_linguistics: The Norman conquest put French participles straight into English verb morphology — countless English past tenses ARE French participles wearing English spelling.
e.philological_note: With avoir, the participle never agrees; with être (motion verbs), it does — the one agreement the past asks for.
e.literature_source: Baugh & Cable, A History of the English Language (2002).

ment.name: The -ment Adverb Bridge
ment.phonetic_rule: English -ly adverbs convert to -ment: exactement, rapidement — the ME is nasal, like pain.
ment.historical_linguistics: Latin -mente ('in a ... mind') became French -ment and English kept the same suffix for nouns (moment, comment) — but French built adverbs with it where English built them with -ly.
ment.philological_note: Feminine adjectives get an -e before -ment: exacte → exactement.

eur.name: The -eur Bridge
eur.phonetic_rule: Latin -or/-er nouns convert to -eur /œʁ/: doctor → docteur, color → couleur.
eur.historical_linguistics: The agent and quality suffixes of Latin split three ways in English (-or, -er, -our) but re-merge in French as -eur.
eur.philological_note: -eur is usually masculine — couleur and erreur are the famous rebels. The lesson names the exceptions before you trust the rule blindly.

able.name: The -able Bridge
able.phonetic_rule: Adjectives in -able/-ible convert as-is: adorable, possible, invisible — only the stress moves.
able.historical_linguistics: Latin -ābilis/-ibilis landed in both languages with the spelling intact; it is the highest-fidelity conversion family in the whole bridge.
able.philological_note: Same form, different stress: invisible with the beat on the final syllable in French.

doublet.name: Norman Doublets
doublet.phonetic_rule: Same Latin word entered English twice — once Germanic-dressed, once Norman: warden/gardien, estate/état, hôtel/hospital.
doublet.historical_linguistics: After 1066 English borrowed Norman French wholesale; centuries of independent drift mean many English words have a French twin that looks different and sounds different but is the same word.
doublet.philological_note: French dropped Latin H everywhere (hôtel, homme) and dropped S before consonants (état, école) — the dropped letters are the fingerprints.
